newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian opposition petitions Chiluba poll victory.
newsitem.headline: Zambian opposition petitions Chiluba poll victory.

text.p: Four Zambian opposition parties filed court petitions on Friday challenging President Frederick Chiluba's landslide victory in disputed polls this month.
In a separate development, two major donor countries -- Japan and Sweden -- rejected accusations by officials that they had bribed monitoring groups to pronounce the elections unfair.

Former president Kenneth Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP), and the Liberal Progressive Front of former legal affairs minister Rodger Chongwe filed a joint petition challenging the president's credentials.
They charged Chiluba lied about his nationality when he filed electoral nomination papers, and said they had evidence that he was of foreign parentage.
As a result of a new constitution passed this year Kaunda was barred from contesting the election because his parents were Malawian. His UNIP party then led a boycott of the polls.

Two other parties, Agenda for Zambia and National Congress, filed a petition challenging the legitimacy of the poll. They claimed an impaired voters' register, which excluded half of the 4.6 million eligible voters, and other irregularities, including vote buying, rendered the elections illegitimate.
"The four parties filed their petitions with the Supreme Court this afternoon," opposition lawyer Sakwiba Sikota told Reuters. No date for their hearing has been set.

The Supreme Court early this month threw out opposition petitions challenging Chiluba's origins because they were filed prematurely. Under new laws effected this year, electoral petitions can only be made after an election has been held.

Some government officials and state media organisations have alleged that diplomats from several donor countries -- including the United States, Britain, Japan and Sweden -- paid the watchdog groups to declare the elections were not free and fair.

"Japan categorically denies the allegations made against Japanese embassy staff...as they are totally baseless, a mere fabrication and a very malicious attempt to defame our good name in Zambia," the Japanese embassy said in a statement.

"Such malevolent, irresponsible allegations may discourage the goodwill of our embassy staff and in turn influence the decline of the mutual friendship and cooperation currently existing between Japan and Zambia," it added.
The Swedish embassy, which funded election monitoring groups, denied it was part of a plot to discredit the polls.
"Linking Sweden to any kind of political plot or accusing her of doctoring monitoring reports is absurd. There are no malevolent intentions behind any of the Swedish...projects."
There was no immediate comment from British or U.S. officials.
The elections office on Friday released final results from the general elections showing that Chiluba won 69 percent of the presidential vote with 913,770 of the 1,258,805 votes cast.
His closest rival, Dean Mungomba of the Zambia Democratic Congress party, got 12 percent of the vote with 160,439 votes.

Mungomba refused to accept the results, charging the polls were rigged by Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy. He went into hiding this week after making statements that police say amount to treason.
